title: The Charge of the Light Brigade
text:
On 25 October 1854, during the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War, the British commander Lord Raglan watched from the heights as Russian troops began hauling away British guns from captured redoubts. He sent an order to his cavalry commander, Lord Lucan, telling the cavalry to advance rapidly to the front and try to prevent the enemy carrying away the guns.

Lucan was in the valley below and could not see what Raglan saw. The order was carried by Captain Louis Nolan, an impatient cavalry officer who despised Lucan. When Lucan asked what guns were meant, Nolan, according to witnesses, waved his arm toward the end of the valley and said, "There, my lord, is your enemy, there are your guns." At the end of that valley stood a Russian battery, with more guns and riflemen on the slopes on both sides.

Lucan passed the order to the commander of the Light Brigade, Lord Cardigan, his brother-in-law, whom he loathed. The two men barely spoke. Cardigan questioned the order, Lucan said it was Raglan's, and Cardigan led about 670 men down the valley. Nolan rode out across the front of the brigade, perhaps trying to redirect it, and was killed by a shell.

The brigade reached the guns and was shattered. More than a hundred men were killed and many more wounded or captured. Watching, the French general Pierre Bosquet is said to have remarked: "It is magnificent, but it is not war."
lesson: Vague orders, poor communication and feuding leaders can destroy a brave team. Make sure instructions are clear and that people who must work together can talk to each other.
people: Lord Raglan, Lord Lucan, Lord Cardigan, Captain Louis Nolan
source: Cecil Woodham-Smith, The Reason Why (1953); contemporary accounts including William Howard Russell's dispatches to The Times
